title: Stem Anatomy and Vascular Transport
objective: Identify the stem tissues that support the canopy and transport water, minerals, sugars, and signals.

terms.definition: Vascular tissue that conducts water and dissolved minerals primarily from roots toward shoots.
Vascular tissue that distributes sugars and other transported compounds between sources and sinks.
A lateral meristem that contributes to secondary vascular growth.
Central stem tissue that can contribute to storage and internal structure.

coreScience: The cannabis stem is both a support column and a transport network. Epidermal and cortical tissues form the outer region of young stems. Vascular bundles contain xylem toward the interior and phloem toward the exterior, with cambial activity contributing to thickening as stems mature. The central region contains pith.

Xylem transport is driven largely by the water-potential gradient created as water evaporates from leaves. A continuous water column, root supply, and intact conducting tissue are required. Phloem moves photosynthates and other compounds from source tissues, often mature leaves, toward growing shoots, roots, flowers, and other sinks.

Bending or cutting a stem changes both mechanical loading and vascular continuity. Plants can reinforce injured areas through wound responses and new tissue, but severe crushing, splitting, constriction, infection, or repeated movement can reduce transport and create entry sites for pathogens.

Stem transport reflects coordinated whole-plant hydraulics and carbon allocation. Xylem is composed largely of dead conducting cells at maturity and functions as a low-resistance pathway for water under tension, while phloem transport depends on living sieve elements and companion cells that load, unload, and maintain pressure-driven flow between sources and sinks. The direction of phloem movement is determined by source-sink relationships rather than a fixed upward or downward rule. As cannabis stems mature, secondary growth and lignification change both mechanical properties and transport capacity.
cultivationRelevance: Support decisions should account for increasing flower mass and lever forces. Stem diameter alone does not guarantee resistance to splitting at branch junctions.
When diagnosing a wilted branch, compare the symptom boundary with the stem. A localized kink, girdle, lesion, or break points toward transport failure rather than a whole-root-zone problem.

Use symptom localization to separate branch-level transport problems from whole-plant root or environment problems. If one branch wilts while neighboring branches remain turgid, inspect the vascular path from that branch back toward the main stem for kinks, ties, splits, lesions, crushing, girdling, or breakage. A whole-canopy wilt suggests a broader hydraulic problem and should shift the investigation toward roots, irrigation, temperature, VPD, or systemic disease.

Training and support systems should prevent constriction as stems thicken. Ties, clips, trellis contact points, and repaired splits need repeated inspection because a support that was safe on a young stem can later compress bark and phloem or concentrate mechanical stress. Record injuries and recovery instead of assuming a visually enlarged callus means vascular function has fully returned.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Measure diameter at a defined node, internode, or height using a consistent instrument and time point. Record whether the stem is primary, lateral, young, or lignified so growth and treatment comparisons use equivalent tissue.

Record branch angle, junction shape, branch length or load, visible included bark or crease, trellis/support contact, and whether the branch is under bending or torsional stress. Photographs from the same orientation improve follow-up.

Record exact location, date, length, approximate depth, crushing, splitting, girdling, discoloration, sap exudation, exposed tissue, contamination risk, and any immediate support or sanitation action. Do not classify a superficial scar and a vascularly disruptive injury as equivalent.

Map whether wilt, chlorosis, necrosis, or growth reduction occurs on one branch, tissue distal to the injury, one side of the plant, or the whole canopy. The anatomical boundary is useful evidence for local versus systemic transport failure.

At repeated intervals record turgor, new growth, lesion expansion, callus or wound tissue, branch angle, support need, and whether symptoms recur under high transpiration or load. A healed surface does not by itself prove full xylem and phloem continuity.

Pair stem symptoms with irrigation status, root-zone condition, temperature, humidity/VPD, recent training, and mechanical events. High transpiration demand can expose partial hydraulic limitations that are less visible under mild conditions.

misconceptions: Xylem pumps water: Water movement depends largely on physical gradients and transpiration, supported by living root processes.
A healed-looking knuckle is always stronger: Appearance does not prove restored transport or resistance to future load.
All stem purple coloration is phosphorus deficiency: Pigmentation can reflect genetics, light, temperature, age, or stress and is not diagnostic alone.
evidenceLimits: Stem anatomy and secondary growth vary with developmental stage, internode position, cultivar, mechanical loading, and selection history, including differences between fiber-oriented and flower-oriented material. General vascular-plant mechanisms describe xylem and phloem function well, but the amount of transport loss caused by a particular cannabis bend, split, tie, or wound cannot be inferred from appearance alone. Functional recovery should be judged from repeated plant response and symptom localization.
